nodes.title: Dashboard open rate proxy: 33% of alerts are acted on within 5 minutes, 58% within an hour, and the gate subset is 5x faster than the rest
nodes.body:
w3-attention-gap-dashboard-open-rate asked for a figure nobody publishes: how often a human opens a dashboard that is available to them. We have the closest analogue in our own record -- every checkpoint is an alert that blocks the loop until a decision, so its raise-to-decision latency is exactly 'did the person act on the thing sitting there'.

Measured with research/exp/e84.mjs over 60 checkpoints in 72 campaigns, all 60 answered:

| acted within | count | share |
|---|---|---|
| 2 min | 9/60 | 15% |
| 5 min | 20/60 | 33% |
| 15 min | 29/60 | 48% |
| 1 h | 35/60 | 58% |
| 4 h | 41/60 | 68% |
| 1 day | 45/60 | 75% |

Full latency: min 34 s, p25 222 s, median 1,326 s, p75 84,976 s, p90 245,439 s, max 76.2 h.

**The kinds must be split**, or this contradicts e67: gate checkpoints have median 261 s (n=25) while all other kinds have median 7,542 s (n=35) -- a 29x difference, and 5x on the 15%-vs-75% share. e67 measured only gate cards and reported 261 s; the all-kind median here is 1,326 s. Both are correct and neither is the answer to 'how fast does the person respond' -- the answer is that they respond fast to the kind they can decide (a diff plus a verdict) and slowly to the kind that needs investigation.

16 of 60 alerts arrived within 60 s of the previous one, confirming the batching observation (exp-gap-013) from the latency side.

nodes.title: Date.parse on an epoch-millisecond number is NaN, and the NaN was filtered out as a missing value
nodes.body:
The event log's `t` field is epoch milliseconds as a number (1794249633742), not an ISO string. research/exp/e84.mjs first computed `Date.parse(e.t)` for both raise and answer times, got NaN for every row, and then filtered `x != null && x >= 0` -- which drops NaN silently. The output was:

  checkpoints raised: 60; answered: 60 (100.0%)
  latency from raise to decision (n=0):
    min NaNs  p25 NaNs  median NaNs ...

i.e. a report that simultaneously claimed all 60 were answered and that zero latencies existed. Two internally inconsistent numbers printed side by side, and neither line threw.

Fixed by using `e.t` directly and adding an assertion: if there are rows but no usable latencies, throw naming the likely cause. That assertion is the general fix -- a count of zero after a filter is a fact about the filter until proven otherwise.

Same family as exp-audit-002 (reading a field that does not exist) and exp-kg-004 (assuming an output format): three silent zeros in one session, all from not asserting the shape of the input before deriving a number from it.
nodes.source: research/exp/e84.mjs first version; event t field is epoch ms

edges.note: answers with a 60-checkpoint latency distribution split by kind
e67's 261s was gate-only; all kinds median 1326s, other kinds 7542s
batching confirmed from the latency side: 16 of 60 within 60s of the previous
third silent zero from an unasserted input shape
